extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy; scholars of early modern epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the methodological principles and provisional moral maxims from Descartes' Discourse on Method (Parts III–V). Focuses on rules for inquiry, standards of certitude, and conduct while pursuing philosophical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to the true order and enumerate all conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The method teaches adherence to the true order, and an exact enumeration of all the conditions of the thing sought; this includes all that gives certitude to the rules of arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes likens the certainty obtained by following true order and enumerating conditions to the certitude of arithmetic. The rule implies solving problems by proceeding in the correct logical order and making sure all relevant conditions are accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare by removing errors and accumulating experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking philosophical inquiry one must eradicate from the mind all the erroneous opinions previously accepted, amass a variety of experience as materials for reasoning, and repeatedly exercise the method to increase skill in its application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes emphasizes a period of preparation and maturation (he delayed some inquiries until older), combining self-critique (clearing prejudices), gathering empirical/material experience, and practice in the method to improve its effective use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory moral maxim I: follow local laws, faith, and moderate opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obey the laws and customs of one's country, adhere to the faith of one's upbringing, and regulate conduct according to the most moderate opinions generally held by the most judicious among those one lives with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the practice of prudent, widely accepted moderate opinions (prefer practice over stated belief), because moderation tends to be more convenient and less likely to be far from truth; avoid binding promises that would prevent future revision of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory moral maxim II: be firm in action; act on the most probable
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as firm and resolute in actions as possible; when truth cannot be determined, act according to what is most probable and thereafter treat that opinion as certain for practical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes uses the traveler analogy: when lost, proceed in a straight line rather than vacillate. This maxim is designed to prevent paralysis of action and remorse from continual change of course when certainty is unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisory moral maxim III: master desires rather than attempt to change the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Endeavor to conquer oneself rather than fortune; change one's desires rather than the order of the world, accepting that only one's own thoughts are truly under control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle aims to produce contentment and prevent futile longing for what is beyond our power. Descartes recommends prolonged discipline and meditation to accustom the mind to this orientation, as practiced by philosophers who remained happy despite external privations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote oneself to cultivation of reason using the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue in the occupation of cultivating reason and progressing in the knowledge of truth by applying the prescribed method; regard this as the best life-work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes views the method as the central project of life: daily discovery of truths using the method yields greater satisfaction than other pursuits and is the foundation for achieving the virtues and goods within one's reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodic doubt: reject any opinion with the least ground for doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: In searching for indubitable truth, reject as absolutely false all opinions in regard to which one can suppose the least ground for doubt, so as to discover what remains wholly indubitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply radical doubt to senses (which sometimes deceive), reasoning (paralogisms can occur), and dreams (experience of thoughts in sleep). The aim is to remove all uncertain beliefs until only certain foundations remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: First indubitable principle: I think, therefore I am (cogito)
rubrics_metrics.description: While doubting everything, it is necessarily certain that the doubting thinker exists: 'I think, therefore I am' is a truth so evident that no sceptical hypothesis can undermine it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes takes the cogito as the foundational certainty from which to begin rebuilding knowledge; it establishes the thinker as a substance whose essence is thought, distinct from the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and distinct perceptions rule
rubrics_metrics.description: All the things which we very clearly and distinctly conceive are true; use clear and distinct conception as the general rule for truth and certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes notes difficulty in determining what counts as 'clear and distinct' but treats such perceptions as the standard of truth. Later he ties their certainty to the existence of a non-deceiving God to secure this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of God as guarantor of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of a supremely perfect Being (God) must have been placed in us by a being more perfect than ourselves; from this, Descartes argues for God's existence and uses it to ground the reliability of clear and distinct ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes reasons that the presence of an idea of infinite perfection cannot come from an imperfect being and so presupposes a perfect cause. Because God is perfect and not a deceiver, the rule that clear and distinct perceptions are true gains metaphysical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileging understanding over imagination and senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on imagination or senses for metaphysical assurance; understanding (intellect) provides assurance where imagination and senses only offer representations limited to material objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes criticizes philosophers who rely on the maxim that nothing is in the understanding that wasn't first in the senses; he insists that ideas like God and the soul are not derived from the senses or imagination and that reason, not imagination, should be the arbiter of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require geometric-level clarity for philosophical propositions; derive laws of nature from God and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept as true only those propositions at least as clear and certain as the demonstrations of geometers; from the principle of God's perfection and clear reasoning, deduce the laws of nature and the structure of the physical world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes sets geometric demonstrations as the benchmark of clarity and intends to reconstruct natural philosophy by assuming a hypothetical new world and deducing how matter, light, heavens, planets, and living beings would arrange themselves under immutable laws impressed by God.
